utterances.text: Let me begin with something you've all seen: those worn tracks across a lawn where people have ignored the paved route.
Planners call them desire paths, and for decades they were treated as a nuisance, evidence that the public couldn't follow instructions.
I want to suggest the opposite reading: that a desire path is free data about how a space is actually used.
Some universities have taken this literally. They leave new lawns unpaved for a year, watch where the tracks appear, and only then lay the pavement.
Now, you might object that this simply rewards impatience. But notice what the alternative costs: fences, signs, and a path nobody uses.
The broader lesson, and this is where I'll spend the rest of today, is that a design which fights its users' habits will usually lose.

utterances.text: Today I'd like to talk about how short naps affect learning.
In one study, students memorized a list of words in the morning. One group then took a twenty-minute nap after lunch, while the other group stayed awake.
When tested in the evening, the nap group remembered about thirty percent more words.
However, longer is not always better. Naps of more than forty minutes often lead to deep sleep, and people who wake from deep sleep feel slow and tired for a while.
Timing matters too. A nap taken after four p.m. tends to delay bedtime, which reduces night-time sleep.
So the general advice is simple: keep naps short, and take them early in the afternoon.
I usually nap for an hour after club practice, around six. Maybe that's why I can't fall asleep until one a.m.
I tried a fifteen-minute nap right after lunch last week, and my afternoon classes felt much easier.
Look at this survey of our school. More than half of the students who nap do it after four.
Then according to the lecture, most of them are probably napping at the wrong time.

utterances.text: Urban Beekeeping.
In recent years, keeping bees on city rooftops has become popular in many countries. Surprisingly, city bees often produce more honey than bees in the countryside.
One reason is that parks and gardens offer a wide variety of flowers throughout the year, while large farms usually grow only one crop.
However, experts warn that the trend has a downside. When too many hives are placed in one area, honeybees compete with wild insects for food, and some wild species have declined as a result.
Some cities now limit the number of hives that can be kept in each district.

utterances.text: The Rebound Effect.
When a technology becomes more efficient, we might expect people to use less energy. Yet economists have long observed the opposite.
In the nineteenth century, William Stanley Jevons noted that as steam engines burned coal more efficiently, coal consumption in Britain actually rose, because cheaper power encouraged new uses.
Today, the same pattern appears with fuel-efficient cars: drivers who spend less per kilometer often drive more.
This does not mean efficiency is pointless.
Researchers argue that it must be paired with policies such as carbon pricing, so that savings are not simply spent on more consumption.

feedback.answer_en: Coal consumption actually rose as engines became more efficient.

utterances.text: Today we're speaking with Naomi Clarke, who restores old books for a national archive. Naomi, what does a typical project involve?
People imagine it's all delicate brushes, but the first week is usually just looking. I document every tear and stain before I touch anything, because whatever I do should be reversible.
Reversible? Why is that so important?

Because techniques improve. Glues that were considered ideal fifty years ago are now damaging the very pages they were meant to save. I'd rather a future conservator be able to undo my work than curse it.
Has digitization changed your job?

It's changed the pressure, not the purpose. Now that scans exist, people handle the originals less, which helps. But a scan can't tell you how a book was sewn or what the paper feels like. If anything, digital copies have made people more curious about the real object.
